//: The shared road-status corpus. BOTH gates are checked against this same
file: tools/draft-lint.test.mjs runs rule 2 over it, and
it. They cannot drift apart on these sentences without one suite failing.
Every case earned its place. PR #35 fixed the composer and the
adjective-first gap; PR #37 unified the two gates, and five review rounds
on it found 31 defects, about two thirds of them regressions introduced
by the previous round's fix. That rate is what this file exists to hold
down: the rules are shallow syntax done with regexes, so a change that
verdict is 'claim' (the gate must flag it) or 'clean' (it must not).
note says what the case guards, so a future failure is legible. Add a
case here rather than to only one suite.

cases.text: Dry roads for the bus run this morning.
cases.note: issue #30, shipped 2026-09-21. Adjective-first, no verb, and about a valley road rather than a pass. system.md forbids 'dry roads for the 6:30 call' by name.

cases.text: Bayfield and up the Pine same story, dry pavement and clear conditions through the morning.
cases.note: issue #30's second sentence.

cases.text: The passes are getting wet pavement at most, maybe a couple inches way up high.
cases.note: issue #34. Present progressive, produced because the brief used to ask for 'what the passes are GETTING'.

cases.text: Not much, maybe a few hundredths, but enough to wet pavement for the evening commute.
cases.note: issue #32 was a LINT false positive: 'wet' here is an infinitive verb, not an adjective.

cases.text: The 501 should be fine this morning but I'd plan for wet roads and maybe some ponding by the afternoon commute home.
cases.note: issue #33 was a LINT false positive: system.md gives "I'd expect" as the prescribed repair.

cases.text: The passes are dry.
cases.note: shipped 2026-09-02, the original.

cases.text: Roads wet, no ice.
cases.note: telegraphic form, forbidden in system.md by name. The lint had no rule for it at all until PR #37.

cases.text: The 160 into town looks fine.
cases.note: forbidden in system.md by name.

cases.text: The 501 and the 240 are both dry for the school run.
cases.note: two roads coordinated; the scan must restart at the second one.

cases.text: Coal Bank and Molas should stay dry through the morning.
cases.note: the thing passes.py exists to do.

cases.text: I'd expect dry pavement by the 6:30 call.
cases.note: system.md's own prescribed repair.

cases.text: That is the forecast, not the road status. Current closures and chain law: https://www.cotrip.org/
cases.note: passes.format_card's boilerplate. 'closures' must not read as 'closed'.

cases.text: Durango and the Animas Valley (6,500') stay dry today with highs in the mid-80s.
cases.note: a bare 501 matches inside (6,500') -- the comma is a word boundary. Weather sentence, no road in it.

cases.text: The Florida is running 160 cfs and the lake is clear this morning.
cases.note: a bare 160 matches 'running 160 cfs'.

cases.text: The 550's closed this morning.
cases.note: the foot-mark exclusion (7,650') must not swallow the possessive.

cases.text: The 501's fine for the bus run.
cases.note: same, on the surface rule.

cases.text: The passes are dry through the morning.
cases.note: a time window says WHEN, never WHETHER. Treating it as a hedge opened a hole.

cases.text: Dry roads all day.
cases.note: the verbless form the rule exists to catch never carries a copula, which is why guarding the time tier on 'present indicative' could not work.

cases.text: Wet pavement through the morning.
cases.note: same shape.

cases.text: The passes should be dry through the morning.
cases.note: the modal, not the time window, is what hedges.

cases.text: Wolf Creek will likely be closed if this verifies.
cases.note: a closure is not hedgeable. Whether a gate is down is CDOT's decision, not weather, so it is not ours to forecast.

cases.text: Red Mountain should be closed by noon.
cases.note: same.

cases.text: The 550 closes at six.
cases.note: plain finite verb.

cases.text: Molas is set to close this afternoon.
cases.note: the infinitive, licensed by the verb in front of it.

cases.text: They expect to close the 550 overnight.
cases.note: reverse order: the road is named after the verb. The lint lacked this pattern until round five.

cases.text: CDOT has closed Molas.
cases.note: asserts a CDOT action.

cases.text: Expect traction law by morning over Wolf Creek.
cases.note: constants.py holds this up as the honest product: a traction law follows from weather we do have. Pinned by tests/test_passes.py too.

cases.text: If CDOT has closed the 550, the detour through Pagosa is long.
cases.note: a weather-contingent conditional makes everything after it contingent.

cases.text: If that band sets up, the 550 is icy by 6am and Molas is slick.
cases.note: same.

cases.text: If you are heading north, Red Mountain is closed.
cases.note: a READER-addressed conditional picks out an audience and then states a flat fact at them.

cases.text: If you're running the 550 this morning, the pass is icy.
cases.note: same, on the surface rule. The opener is dropped before the clause is judged, because 'if' is also a modal hedge.

cases.text: If you are running the 550 today, check CDOT before you go.
cases.note: reader-addressed advice with no claim in it. Pinned by tests/test_passes.py.

cases.text: If you're getting out on a trail today its a good window for it.
The 550 is icy if that band sets up.
cases.note: a trailing subordinator is the one thing that scopes BACKWARDS, unlike a modal.

cases.text: Roads are wet and it should dry out by noon.
cases.note: a modal governs what FOLLOWS it. Report-then-advice is commoner than modal-first and was un-gated when the hedge was asked per clause.

cases.text: I'd expect wet pavement in town and icy roads for the bus run.
cases.note: 'run' is a noun: 'bus run' and 'school run' appear 33 times in the recorded corpus and in clean.md.

cases.text: I'd expect wet pavement in town but icy roads on the 550.
cases.note: 'but' coordinates objects as often as clauses.

cases.text: The front should clear by noon; roads wet and icy on the 550.
cases.note: a semicolon joins independent statements; the modal does not reach past it.

cases.text: Coal Bank should stay dry, and Molas is clear right now.
cases.note: with the comma the persona usually writes, the second claim is judged on its own.

cases.text: Coal Bank should stay dry and Molas is clear right now.
cases.note: THE KNOWN MISS, deliberate. Without the comma this is one hedged clause. Three rounds went into carrying a hedge across a coordination and every version was wrong, because telling a second predicate from a second object needs to tell a noun from a verb. A false flag on the phrasing compose.py prescribes cannot be repaired by the rewrite loop, so it is the more expensive error. If a change makes this a claim again, check it has not also re-broken the 'bus run' case above.

cases.text: The cold front passes through around noon, closing out the showers.
cases.note: 'passes' is also the verb for weather moving through, and 'closing out' is about showers.

cases.text: The storm passes overnight and clears by dawn.
cases.note: same.

cases.text: The high passes are closed this morning.
cases.note: requiring the determiner adjacent missed this.

cases.text: The passes over the divide are closed.
cases.note: a guard list of 'words only a moving system takes' threw this away -- those are ordinary prepositions after the noun.

cases.text: Passes are closed.
cases.note: bare, unambiguous because a copula follows.

cases.text: The passes get icy.
cases.note: `gets` reached the pass lookahead and the lint before it reached _ROAD_STATE_CLAIM, so the early gate was weaker than the late one.

cases.text: Coal Bank and Molas are close to the freezing line this morning.
cases.note: 'close' is the adjective. Because closures are hedge-exempt, matching it was an unrecoverable flag on the product's signature sentence.

cases.text: The snow line drops down to close to 11,000 feet on the passes.
cases.note: same, through the infinitive branch.

cases.text: The snow line will be close to 11,000 feet on the passes.
cases.note: same, through the modal branch -- an optional 'be' re-admitted it once.

cases.text: That adds up to close to a foot on Red Mountain by morning.
cases.note: a spelled-out amount. An allowlist of what may follow 'close to' kept letting one shape through, so the infinitive is licensed by the verb in front instead.

cases.text: Red Mountain is set to close to traffic at six.
cases.note: and that licensing must not throw away the real closure.

cases.text: Molas and Coal Bank both pick up snow and the districts may close.
cases.note: the subject changes at the 'and', so a proximity window may not cross it. Cited in road_status_claim's own docstring.

cases.text: Snow piles up on Red Mountain and the window is clear.
cases.note: same, on the surface rule. The lint had no proximity bound at all.

cases.text: That's heavy enough to make the 240 and the upper 501 slick this evening.
cases.note: 2026-09-22 again. A forecast consequence, and in a 5:45am post 'this evening' is the future where 'this morning' is now.

cases.text: All clear over Molas and Coal Bank.
cases.note: the surface word first. Lost entirely when a duplicate rule set was deleted.

cases.text: Red Mountain bare to the top.
cases.note: an adjective before a preposition still ends the claim.

cases.text: Vallecito Road, fine gravel past the turn.
cases.note: and an adjective before a NOUN does not -- this is an ordinary noun phrase.

cases.text: Red Mountain all clear this morning.
cases.note: a trailing present-tense time word does not end the claim either.

cases.text: The 550 is currently dry.
cases.note: 'currently' was only in the deleted duplicate's prefix list.
